profile.name: Sadi Moma
profile.tagline: An open-circle Bulgarian line dance set to a 7/8 rhythm about a girl planting vines.
profile.insight: Danced to a Bulgarian 7/8 meter counted as slow-quick-quick, the melody of Sadi Moma was later adapted by Richard Stallman to write the Free Software Song.
profile.profile: Sadi Moma is a traditional Bulgarian folk dance and accompanying song performed in open circles with dancers holding hands in a high W-position. The music follows an asymmetrical 7/8 time signature with a slow-quick-quick rhythmic feel. The song's lyrics narrate a story about a girl who plants a grapevine that yields nine barrels of wine and one of rakija, which a young soldier drinks away alongside his horse. It remains a classic example of Bulgarian folk heritage with widespread cultural recognition.
profile.profile_long:
Sadi Moma, translating to 'A Girl Plants', represents a well-known Bulgarian folk tradition where music and movement are closely interwoven. Rooted in the rich rural folklore of Bulgaria, the tradition centres on a narrative song paired with a collective circle dance. The narrative tells of a young girl who plants a white wine grapevine, briefly regretting her labor before it produces a massive yield—nine barrels of wine and a tenth barrel of clear, potent rakija. The story takes a dramatic turn when a young soldier discovers the haul and goes on a week-long drinking spree, eventually gambling or drinking away his own black horse. This blend of agricultural labor, humor, and cautionary storytelling is typical of traditional Eastern European song-dance genres.

In performance, Sadi Moma brings dancers together in one or multiple open circles, a classic spatial arrangement for Balkan line and circle dances. Participants maintain continuous contact through held hands positioned in a W-position, elevated at shoulder level. This upper-body connection helps stabilize the line as dancers navigate the distinctive metric structure of the accompaniment. The spatial pathway moves dynamically along the arc of the open circle, led by the dancer at the open end of the line.

Musically, Sadi Moma is defined by its uneven or additive meter. It is written in 7/8 time, structured internally into a three-part rhythmic division of slow-quick-quick (SQQ). Dancers and musicians internalize this meter as an elongated first beat followed by two shorter beats. The driving folk melody gained unexpected global recognition in modern digital culture when programmer and activist Richard Stallman borrowed its tune to compose the anthem for the free software movement, the 'Free Software Song'.

As a living artifact of Bulgarian expressive culture, Sadi Moma demonstrates how traditional folk dance uses communal spatial structures and asymmetric rhythms to engage dancers across generations. While the song text preserves traditional village imagery of grape harvests and soldier tales, the accompanying dance offers an accessible yet rhythmically precise entry into the complex world of Balkan folk choreographies.

sections.origins_and_history: Sadi Moma originated in Bulgaria as a traditional folk song and associated folk dance. The title translates to 'A Girl Plants', referring to the opening lyrics of the narrative folk song. Over time, the tune became a recognized piece of Bulgarian heritage and notably crossed into modern culture when Richard Stallman adapted its melody for the Free Software Song.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance is performed in one or more open circles of dancers. Dancers join hands and hold their arms in a W-position at shoulder level. The movement follows the asymmetrical 7/8 meter of the music, which is counted in a slow-quick-quick pattern. Specific footwork details and step names are not described in sources.
sections.music_and_instruments: The dance is set to the Bulgarian folk song Sadi Moma, written in an uneven 7/8 meter. The rhythm is divided as slow-quick-quick (SQQ). The narrative lyrics describe a girl planting a white wine grapevine that produces nine barrels of wine and one barrel of strong rakija, which a young soldier drinks until he loses his horse. Specific musical instruments are not described in sources.
sections.costume_and_setting: Traditional settings and specific traditional Bulgarian costumes worn during the dance are not described in sources.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The song's narrative reflects village life, agriculture, and folk humor, detailing the regret and reward of agricultural work (planting vines) followed by a cautionary tale of a soldier's binge drinking. It serves as social folk recreation in line and circle formations.
sections.notable_figures: Richard Stallman is noted for borrowing the traditional melody of Sadi Moma to write the Free Software Song.
sections.regional_variants: Specific regional variations or alternate choreographies across different provinces of Bulgaria are not described in sources.
sections.lineage: Classified as a Bulgarian folk dance and song within the broader family of Balkan folk dances featuring open-circle formations and additive asymmetrical meters (7/8).

basic_steps: Form an open circle facing inward or along the line of direction.
Join hands with neighboring dancers and raise arms into a W-position at shoulder height.
Step according to the 7/8 meter following the slow-quick-quick (SQQ) rhythmic pulse.
teaching.level_notes: Accessible for beginners learning Balkan asymmetrical meters due to the clear slow-quick-quick 7/8 division and supportive W-position arm hold.

music_profile.vocal_style: Traditional Bulgarian folk vocal style singing a narrative story
music_profile.sound_description: A traditional Bulgarian melody in asymmetrical 7/8 time. The rhythm is characterized by a distinct slow-quick-quick pulse underlying a strophic narrative folk vocal line.

movement_profile.posture: Upright posture with arms joined in a high W-position
movement_profile.arms_and_hands: Arms joined with neighboring dancers in a W-position
movement_profile.formation_and_space: One or more open circles moving in a line structure
movement_profile.partnering: Group connection via joined hands in W-position; no individual partnering
movement_profile.tempo_feel: Asymmetrical 7/8 pulse with a slow initial beat followed by two quick beats
movement_profile.what_to_avoid: Dropping the W-position hand hold or miscounting the asymmetrical 7/8 slow-quick-quick meter

episode_brief.title_hook: Rhythms of the Balkan Grapevine: Sadi Moma
episode_brief.logline: Explore how a Bulgarian folk song in 7/8 time brings communities into open-circle dances and inspired an iconic piece of tech culture.
beats: Introduction to the narrative song 'Sadi Moma' and its tale of grape vines and a soldier's indulgence.
Demonstration of the open-circle spatial formation and the W-position hand hold.
Breakdown of the asymmetric 7/8 meter into slow-quick-quick pulses.
Connecting the traditional movement line with the sung narrative rhythm.
A look at the unexpected modern connection: how the melody became Richard Stallman's Free Software Song.

lesson_ladder.goal: Master the W-position hand hold and internalize the 7/8 meter
drills: Clap the slow-quick-quick (SQQ) 7/8 rhythm along with the vocal melody.
Practice holding the W-position with partners while stepping on the spot to the SQQ count.

claims.text: Sadi Moma is a Bulgarian folk song in an uneven 7/8 meter counted as slow-quick-quick.
claims.quote: Sadi Moma ("A Girl Plants") is a Bulgarian folk song. The song, like many Bulgarian and other traditional Eastern European folk songs, is in an uneven meter: 7/8, counted as slow-quick-quick (SQQ).

claims.text: There is a Bulgarian folk dance associated with Sadi Moma danced in open circles with arms in a W-position.
claims.quote: There is a Bulgarian folk dance traditionally associated with the song Sadi Moma and often called by the same name. It is danced in one or more open circles of dancers, whose arms are joined in W-position.

claims.text: Richard Stallman borrowed the melody of Sadi Moma for the Free Software Song.
claims.quote: Its melody was borrowed by Richard Stallman for the tune of the Free Software Song.

claims.text: The English translation of Sadi Moma describes a girl planting a vine that filled barrels with wine and rakija.
claims.quote: A girl planted a vine, a white wine grape vine. For one day she planted, for two she regretted the white wine grape vine. The vine grew up, the white wine grape vine. It filled nine barrels with wine, The tenth with clear, strong rakija.

claims.text: The song's story includes a young soldier who drank for a week and drank up his horse.
claims.quote: A young soldier learned to drink. He drank for two days, he drank for three days, for a week. He drank up his black horse from under him.

claims.text: Wikidata classifies Sadi Moma as a folk dance and musical work.
